clue.text: Picture what happens when clouds collapse and fusion occurs

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a film, the musical remade several times in Hollywood

definitions.text: what happens when clouds collapse and fusion occurs
definitions.meaning: second meaning: gas clouds collapsing under gravity until nuclear fusion ignites is how a sun forms

explanation.surface: A science lesson describing the birth of a sun in deep space.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Picture' looks like an instruction to imagine the scene, but it is the film. The rest reads literally as astronomy.
explanation.definitionFit: The title names a famous movie, and a movie is a picture in the older cinema sense, while the phrase also literally describes stellar formation.

clue.text: Remarkably short sentence with lesson part translated

indicators.note: translating turns words into a different form, so these letters are rendered in a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A grammar teacher translating part of a lesson produces a notably brief sentence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sentence' reads as grammar, but the definition means a punishment from a judge; 'with' is part of the letters, not a joining word.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes a very lenient punishment, the kind a court hands down when it barely penalises an offender.

clue.text: Area found in cybercafe, going upstairs?

indicators.note: in a down clue, going upstairs means travelling from bottom to top, so the letters read backwards
something found in a longer word is sitting inside it, waiting to be picked out

parts.note: the run of letters in the middle of the word

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether the seating area of an internet cafe is on the upper floor.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down entry, 'going upstairs' means the letters climb, so the hidden run is read from bottom to top.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a unit of land measurement, roughly 4,047 square metres, so it is a standard example of an area.

clue.text: Ate from tin with edges warped

indicators.note: something warped is bent out of its proper shape, so the letters are distorted into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone eats straight out of a dented can whose rim is bent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'from' and 'with' only join; 'edges' is part of the letters, not the rim of the can.
explanation.definitionFit: To ingest is to take food into the body by swallowing, a slightly clinical synonym for eating.

clue.text: After friend, acquire discount

indicators.note: one thing coming after another means the second piece follows the first in sequence

parts.note: bud is informal American for a pal
to get something is to acquire it

explanation.surface: Once you have a pal on the inside, you can get a reduced price.
explanation.walkthrough: 'discount' is an adjective here, as in a discount airline, not a noun or verb.
explanation.definitionFit: As an adjective, the word describes cheap, low-cost goods or services, as in budget flights or budget hotels.

clue.text: Dig finds nothing buried in folly

indicators.note: something buried in something else lies wholly inside it, so one piece sits within another

parts.note: rot is foolish nonsense
the figure zero, shaped like the letter

explanation.surface: An archaeological excavation of a garden folly turns up nothing at all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'folly' suggests a garden ornament building, but here it means foolishness.
explanation.definitionFit: Pigs root and people root around, both meaning to rummage or turn over soil while searching.

clue.text: Hollywood actor, old player then so active

indicators.note: active letters are lively and moving about rather than staying put in order

parts.note: Bobby and Jack Charlton were England's 1966 World Cup-winning footballing brothers
these six letters rearranged

explanation.surface: A film star who used to play a sport stays fit in later life.
explanation.walkthrough: The Charlton brothers were famous English footballers of the 1960s; the actor is the star of Ben-Hur.
explanation.definitionFit: He was an American film star of epics such as Ben-Hur and The Ten Commandments, working in Hollywood.

clue.text: What a dozy person may do — cancel plans to host a dancing event?

definitions.text: What a dozy person may do
definitions.meaning: first meaning: to make a careless mistake through inattention

definitions.text: cancel plans to host a dancing event
definitions.meaning: second meaning, read literally: to scrap a formal dance from the programme

explanation.surface: A sleepy organiser calls off the dance they were meant to be running.
explanation.walkthrough: The idiom is read once figuratively and once literally, with a ball as a formal dance.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to blunder or fail at a task through carelessness, which is typical of someone half asleep.

clue.text: Just untrustworthy, the dog, or my generous spirit?

indicators.note: untrustworthy letters cannot be relied on to stay in their stated order

parts.note: just and fair both mean equitable
these ten letters rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether their dog is a rogue or a kind-hearted soul.
explanation.walkthrough: 'spirit' suggests a mood or a drink, but it is a magical being here; 'Just' means fair, not only.
explanation.definitionFit: In fairy tales such as Cinderella this magical figure grants wishes and gifts, a benevolent supernatural being.

clue.text: Consequences, for example, when a leg or arm up for treatment

indicators.note: things sent for treatment are worked on and reshaped, so these letters are reworked

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A hospital scene: the consequences of an injured leg or arm raised for treatment.
explanation.walkthrough: Consequences is an old British indoor game in which players add lines to a story on folded paper without seeing earlier lines.
explanation.definitionFit: Consequences is one example of the traditional indoor games played in a drawing room at family gatherings.

clue.text: Missing, a trough returned

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: something returned goes back the way it came, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: a trough is a low point, as in peaks and troughs

explanation.surface: A lost animal feeding trough has been brought back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'trough' suggests a feeding container, but it is a low point, as on a graph.
explanation.definitionFit: The military abbreviation for absent without leave describes a soldier who has gone missing from duty.

clue.text: Somewhat joyless existence in English county

indicators.note: somewhat means to some extent, so only a portion of the following words is used

parts.note: the end of the first word runs into the start of the second

explanation.surface: Life is a bit bleak in a particular part of England.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface invites a dig at the county, but the answer simply spans the two words.
explanation.definitionFit: It is one of the counties of England, lying north-east of London on the North Sea coast.

clue.text: Mouth in river covered by water supplier

indicators.note: something covered by another thing is enclosed by it, so one piece goes inside another

parts.note: a tap supplies water
R is the standard abbreviation for river

explanation.surface: A river estuary sits under a water company's control.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mouth in river' suggests an estuary, but 'Mouth' stands alone as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Trap is slang for someone's mouth, as in the instruction to shut your trap and stop talking.

clue.text: Informative novel, surprisingly vacuous

parts.note: novel as an adjective means new

indicators.note: vacuous means empty, so the word is emptied of everything but its outside letters

parts.note: the first and last letters of the word

explanation.surface: A book review: the novel was informative, yet oddly empty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'novel' looks like a book, but it is the adjective meaning fresh.
explanation.definitionFit: Newsy describes a letter or chat full of news, so it is full of information and updates.

clue.text: Ship not starting on time, still

indicators.note: a thing not starting has lost its beginning, so the opening letter goes

parts.note: a liner is a passenger ship; lose its first letter
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: A ship has failed to set off at the scheduled hour and remains in port.
explanation.walkthrough: 'still' looks like 'nevertheless', but it is the adjective meaning motionless.
explanation.definitionFit: Inert describes something lacking motion or activity, so it is a synonym for motionless or unmoving.

clue.text: Washed with soap, youth's quarantined in that place

indicators.note: to be quarantined in is to be shut away inside, so one piece is enclosed by another

parts.note: a lad is a youth
there means in that place

explanation.surface: A boy scrubbed clean while isolated somewhere during an epidemic.
explanation.walkthrough: Read ''s' as 'has': the youth has that place quarantined inside him.
explanation.definitionFit: To lather is to rub foam over, so being covered in suds means having been cleaned using soap.

clue.text: Take some notes

definitions.meaning: second meaning: a brief fragment of a song or tune

explanation.walkthrough: It reads like a lecture-hall instruction to write things down, but the notes are musical.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb it means grab or seize, and as a noun a short burst of music overheard, like a few bars.

clue.text: Left-hander stirring soup with what?

indicators.note: stirring mixes things around, so the letters are jumbled into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone left-handed is stirring soup and is asked what utensil they are using.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters are those of 'soup' and 'what'; 'with' simply joins them.
explanation.definitionFit: Southpaw is informal, originally American, for a left-handed person, especially a boxer or baseball pitcher.

clue.text: Nervous — and difficult?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: anxious, ill at ease
second meaning, read as prefix plus adjective: not simple

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the second meaning as a whimsical split: 'un-' plus a word for simple.
explanation.definitionFit: The word usually means anxious, but taken apart as a negated adjective it means not simple, so hard.

clue.text: Handle OK, or loose? Stick rotated to secure it

indicators.note: turning something round makes it face the other way, so the letters run backwards
securing something means holding it fast, so one piece is gripped inside another

parts.note: to bond is to stick together

indicators.note: loose things are not fixed in place, so these letters are free to move

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A DIY question: is the handle fine or wobbly? Twist the rod to fix it in place.
explanation.walkthrough: 'it' refers to the jumbled letters, which the turned-round word holds inside.
explanation.definitionFit: A round grip on a door is turned to open it, so it is one kind of handle.

clue.text: Pen in pink circling error, finally

indicators.note: circling something means going all the way round it, so one piece surrounds another

parts.note: coral is a pinkish-orange colour

indicators.note: finally points to the end, so only the closing letter is taken

parts.note: the last letter

explanation.surface: A teacher writing in pink ink circles a mistake at the end of an essay.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pen' looks like a writing tool to go with the ink, but it is an animal enclosure.
explanation.definitionFit: A corral is an enclosure for horses or cattle, the same thing as a livestock pen.

clue.text: Dress old actress shortened

indicators.note: something shortened has been cut down, so its final letter is dropped

parts.note: Greta Garbo, the Swedish star of 1930s Hollywood, minus her last letter

explanation.surface: A veteran actress's frock has been taken up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dress' reads as a noun for a frock, which fits; it could also be a verb, but the answer is the noun for clothing.
explanation.definitionFit: Garb means clothing, especially of a distinctive kind, so it is a synonym for attire or costume.

clue.text: Cracked waste receptacle

definitions.meaning: second meaning: a child's chamber pot for toilet training

explanation.surface: A broken rubbish bin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cracked' suggests damage to the bin, but it means crazy in British slang.
explanation.definitionFit: In British slang the word means eccentric or mad, and it is also the small pot a toddler uses as a toilet.

clue.text: Phone broken by a bird

indicators.note: a thing broken by another is split open with the intruder lodged inside

parts.note: tel. is the abbreviation for telephone
taken as written

explanation.surface: A telephone smashed by a bird.
explanation.walkthrough: TEL is the standard abbreviation for telephone, as printed on letterheads and business cards.
explanation.definitionFit: The teal is a small freshwater duck, so it is a straightforward example of a bird.

clue.text: Blade cut roof from tent

indicators.note: in a down entry the roof is the top, so the first letter is removed

parts.note: a tepee is a conical tent; drop its first letter

explanation.surface: Someone uses a knife to slice the top off a tent.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue the 'roof' is the top letter.
explanation.definitionFit: The epee is a fencing sword, so it counts as a blade in the sporting sense.

clue.text: Riddle is written up on paper

indicators.note: in a down entry, written up means set down from bottom to top, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: taken as written
the Financial Times, a British newspaper, is known as the FT

explanation.surface: A puzzle has been set down on a sheet of paper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Riddle' looks like a puzzle, but a riddle is also a coarse sieve, and to riddle is to sieve.
explanation.definitionFit: To riddle soil or gravel is to pass it through a coarse sieve, which is exactly to separate it by sieving.

clue.text: Lift rugby player in Paris team I battered

indicators.note: one thing in another sits inside it, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: these ten letters rearranged

indicators.note: something battered is knocked out of shape, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: a prop is a front-row forward in rugby

explanation.surface: A rugby forward hoists a teammate in a French side that the speaker has just beaten.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lift' suggests a line-out lift in rugby, but it means steal.
explanation.definitionFit: Lift is informal for steal, and to misappropriate is to take dishonestly what belongs to another, such as funds.

clue.text: Chicken put to death in national park

parts.note: chicken and yellow both mean cowardly
to stone is to execute by throwing rocks

explanation.surface: A chicken is killed inside a national park.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chicken' looks like a bird, but it is the adjective meaning cowardly.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the famous American reserve in Wyoming, the world's first protected area of its kind, known for geysers.
